problem_type: Signal race while a gates-lock wrapper starts its foreground child
symptom: When SIGTERM lands between subprocess.Popen and signal-handler installation, the wrapper exits with signal status null instead of 143 and leaves its detached child running with the shared gates lock descriptor.
direct_cause: scripts/with-gates-lock.py execute() installs SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers only after Popen returns, so the default signal action can terminate the wrapper during child creation before it can kill the child process group.
class_root: The shared child-spawn boundary has no invariant that cancellation handlers are installed before every Popen call and that a signal arriving before the child exists is replayed immediately after Popen returns.
affected_population: Every local gates, test, walkthrough, and other package.json entrypoint using scripts/with-gates-lock.py
Direct, inherited nested, and queued admissions that converge on execute()
POSIX runs where detached foreground process groups inherit the lock descriptor, with the same pre-spawn ordering requirement on Windows

internal_only_reason: The invariant is owned by this repository's Python wrapper around the standard-library subprocess, signal, and OS process-group primitives; no third-party dependency controls the ordering.
invariants: SIGTERM and SIGINT handlers are installed before every execute() Popen call.
A signal received before Popen returns is recorded, then immediately applied to the returned child using the existing Windows terminate or POSIX killpg branch.
The wrapper preserves the existing 128 + signum exit status and closes its lock descriptor so the next admission can acquire it.

prevention.invariant: Every child-starting execute() call has SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers installed first, and a signal observed before Popen returns is replayed immediately after child creation through the existing platform termination branch.
prevention.failure_mode: The child is terminated or its POSIX process group is killed, wait returns the original 128 + signum status, and main closes the lock descriptor; no sleep, retry, or alternate fallback path is added.
prevention.strategy: Move the handler setup to the earliest shared execute() boundary, retain a pending signum until child assignment, and replay it immediately after Popen. The old post-Popen-only ordering is removed in the same change.

legacy_paths.rationale: The old ordering that installed cancellation handlers only after Popen is deleted in place; there is no fallback execute path or second wrapper implementation.

dependency_lifecycle.rationale: The invariant is implemented with the existing Python standard library and OS primitives; no third-party runtime controls signal delivery or process-group ownership.

migration: No user-data or lock-file migration is needed. Existing lock and queue files remain valid; only the in-memory child-start lifecycle changes.
residual_risks: Windows-specific signal delivery and terminate behavior remain unexecuted on this macOS host; the pre-Popen handler invariant is structural and the existing Windows terminate branch is preserved.

A signal that arrives after the pending replay but before wait still follows the existing installed handler and platform termination path; this change does not add retries or alter child exit semantics.

invariant_owner_layer.why: All lock-protected entrypoints converge on execute(), where handler installation, pending replay, child-group termination, and exit mapping can be enforced together.
